## Dataset Challenges: Generalization Across Cameras and Animals This dataset is intentionally designed to evaluate **model generalization under realistic farm conditions**. The primary challenge arises from **distribution shifts** between training and testing data, including changes in **camera viewpoints, scene geometry, illumination, time period, and animal appearance**. **Training Set 1 (T1)** represents the most challenging setting: models trained on T1 have **never seen the camera viewpoints or pig batches used in the test set**, requiring robust cross-view and cross-animal generalization. **Training Set 2 (T2)** relaxes this constraint by adding a small number of images (**~4.5% of the test set size**) captured from the **same camera viewpoints as the test set**, while still ensuring that **no test-set pigs are included**. This provides limited **camera-view context** without introducing subject overlap, allowing models to better adapt to target scene geometry and perspective. The performance gap between T1 and T2 highlights the difficulty of **viewpoint generalization** and emphasizes the importance of learning posture representations that are robust to camera-dependent variations rather than memorizing animal-specific cues. ## Dataset Folder and File Structure The multiview_pig_posture_recognition directory has the following subfolder and file structure: ``` multiview_pig_posture_recognition/ ├── train1_images/ # Training set 1 images │ ├── pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204.jpg │ ├── pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085209.jpg │ └── ... ├── train2_images/ # Training set 2 images │ ├── pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204.jpg │ ├── pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085209.jpg │ └── ... ├── test_images/ # Test images │ ├── pen1_tur_cam1_20250920_174649.jpg │ ├── pen1_tur_cam1_20250921_050022.jpg │ └── ... ├── train1.csv # Training set 1 annotations (bbox + posture labels) ├── train2.csv # Training set 2 annotations (bbox + posture labels) ├── test.csv # Test annotations (bbox only) ├── sample_submission.csv # Example submission format └── pig_posture_classes.txt # Mapping of class IDs to posture names ``` --- ## Training Annotations Each row in the 'train1.csv' and 'train2.csv' files corresponds to **one pig instance** (one bounding box) of a train image. ### Columns | Column | Description | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | row_id | Unique identifier for each pig instance | | image_id | Image filename (e.g., pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204.jpg) | | width, height | Original image dimensions (pixels) | | bbox | Bounding box in [xmin, ymin, w, h] format (absolute pixel units) | | class_id | Posture class ID (0–4) | ### Example ```csv row_id,image_id,width,height,bbox,class_id train_pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204_0000,pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204.jpg,1920,1080,[967.5,331.5,463.0,447.0],3 ``` ## Filename Pattern Image filenames follow the pattern: ``` pen-number_camera-type_camera-number_date_time_instance-id.file-extension ``` **Example:** ``` pen1_orb_cam1_20250108_085204.jpg ``` ### Filename Components | Component | Description | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | `pen-number` | Pig pen identifier (e.g., `pen1`, `pen2`) | | `camera-type` | Camera model (`orb` = Orbbec, `tur` = Turret) | | `camera-number` | Camera index (e.g., `cam1`, `cam2`) | | `date_time` | Capture timestamp in `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS` format | | `file-extension` | Image file format (e.g., `.jpg`) |
**Note:** Bounding box coordinates are provided in **absolute pixel units** relative to the original image resolution and are **not normalized**. --- ## Test Set (`test.csv`) All test images are provided in the `/test_images` directory. The `test.csv` file contains **ground-truth bounding boxes only** (no posture labels). Participants must **predict the posture class for each bounding box listed in `test.csv`**. Ground-truth posture labels for the test set are **hidden** and used exclusively for leaderboard evaluation. --- ## Evaluation Metric Submissions are evaluated using the **macro-averaged F1 score**, computed across the five posture classes. A prediction is considered correct if: * The predicted posture class matches the ground-truth label for the corresponding **pig instance (`row_id`)** Macro-F1 assigns **equal importance to all posture classes**, making it suitable for class imbalance. --- ## Submission Format A sample submission file, sample_submission.csv, is provided for reference. Each submission must be a CSV file containing exactly two columns, formatted as follows: | Column | Description | | ---------- | -------------------------------------- | | `row_id` | Unique pig instance ID from `test.csv` | | `class_id` | Predicted posture class (integer 0–4) | ### Example ```csv row_id,class_id test_pen1_tur_cam1_20250920_174649_0000,0 test_pen1_tur_cam1_20250920_174649_0001,1 ``` Ensure that:
  • All row_id values exactly match those provided in test.csv.
  • Each row_id appears once and only once in the submission file.
## Pig Posture Classes The file pig_posture_classes.txt defines the mapping between posture class IDs and their corresponding pig posture labels. Each line represents one posture class, with the line index indicating the class ID. Class Definitions: 0 — Lateral_lying_left 1 — Lateral_lying_right 2 — Sitting 3 — Standing 4 — Sternal_lying ## Notes * Bounding boxes are **axis-aligned** and provided for **both training and test sets** * Multiple pigs may appear in a single image * Participants **do not need to predict bounding boxes** * The task focuses purely on **instance-level posture classification under real-world farm conditions** ---

Accurate detection of pig posture in real farm environments remains a challenging problem in computer vision. Unlike controlled laboratory settings, commercial barns present cluttered backgrounds, frequent occlusions, variable lighting conditions, and diverse camera viewpoints. In addition, several pig postures exhibit subtle visual differences, making posture discrimination from 2D images particularly difficult. This competition aims to advance pig posture recognition by encouraging the development and evaluation of deep learning models in multi-view scenes under realistic farm conditions. It also addresses the difficulty in generalizing detections to different pigs and different cameras from those used in the training set. All data were collected from two pig pens at the Swine Research Center, Michigan State University. Images were acquired using eight overhead cameras and include multiple pig breeds (Purebred Yorkshire, Exotic crossbred, and Meishan) across different production batches. There are two training sets and one *Test Set*: * **Training Set 1** contains 3,090 images captured from five camera views, with a total of 22,934 annotated posture instances. * **Training Set 2** adds 60 images from testing set camera views and so comprises 3,150 images with 23,450 posture instances. The camera array used in data collection ![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F29008476%2Fb2b6dc1d276b1698f1abb01a1c76ccec%2Fleaderboard_camera.png?generation=1767893280056824&alt=media) The training dataset statistics ![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F29008476%2F8b42bf6941e40f45c8686df5a1b61d3f%2Ftrain1_vs_train2_hist.png?generation=1767984424131922&alt=media) Each pen contains 8 to 10 pigs per batch. For every pig instance, the dataset provides an axis-aligned bounding box (xmin, ymin, w, h) in both the training and test sets. However, posture labels are available only for the training set. Participants are required to predict the posture for each detected pig instance in the test set and submit their results using a standard submission CSV file, which will be automatically evaluated and ranked on the leaderboard. The task is to classify the posture of each pig into one of the following five categories: - Lateral_lying_left - Lateral_lying_right - Sitting - Standing - Sternal_lying ## Dataset Challenges: Generalization Across Cameras and Animals > *“Generalization across unseen camera views and animals remains a core challenge in posture recognition.”* This dataset is curated to evaluate **model generalization under realistic farm conditions**. The primary challenge arises from **distribution shifts** between training and testing data, including changes in **camera viewpoints, scene geometry, time period, and animal appearance**. **Training Set 1 (T1)** represents the most challenging setting: models trained on T1 have **never seen the camera viewpoints or pig batches used in the test set**, requiring robust cross-view and cross-animal generalization. **Training Set 2 (T2)** relaxes this constraint by adding a small number of images (**~4.5% of the test set size**) captured from the **same camera viewpoints as the test set**, while still ensuring that **no test-set pigs are included**. This provides limited **camera-view context** without introducing subject overlap, allowing models to better adapt to target scene geometry and perspective. The performance gap between T1 and T2 highlights the difficulty of **viewpoint generalization** and emphasizes the importance of learning posture representations that are robust to camera-dependent variations rather than memorizing animal-specific cues. By participating in this challenge, you will not only test your skills in instance-level image classification, representation learning, and model generalization between the camera views and pig batches, but also contribute to ongoing research in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) an emerging interdisciplinary field where machine learning, sensor technology, and animal science converge to enable smarter, more sustainable livestock production systems. The ultimate goal is to build a robust and generalizable posture recognition model that performs consistently across different camera devices, viewpoints, pig batches, pig populations, and environmental conditions.

Submissions are evaluated using the macro-averaged F1 score. This metric computes the F1 score independently for each posture class and then averages the scores, giving equal weight to all classes regardless of their frequency. This makes it particularly suitable for imbalanced datasets. 
F1 = 2 × (precision × recall) / (precision + recall)
Scores range from 0.0 to 1.0, where 1.0 indicates perfect classification performance, and 0.0 indicates no correct predictions. The final competition ranking is based on the private leaderboard, which is evaluated using a Solution CSV file. ## Submission Format Each submission must be a CSV file with **two columns**: | Column | Description | | ---------- | -------------------------------------- | | `row_id` | Unique pig instance ID from `test.csv` | | `class_id` | Predicted posture class (integer 0–4) | ### Example ```csv row_id,class_id test_pen1_tur_cam1_20250920_174649_0000,0 test_pen1_tur_cam1_20250920_174649_0001,1 ``` Must exactly match the row_id of test.csv. - label An integer value from 0 to 4, corresponding to the following posture classes:
Class ID Posture Name
0Lateral_lying left
1Lateral_lying right
2Sitting
3Standing
4Sternal_lying
## Submission Naming Requirement (Mandatory) To clearly distinguish model performance across the two training sets, **all submissions must follow the naming convention specified below**. ### Required Submission Name Format Participants must submit **two separate entries**, one for each training set, using the following prefixes: * **`T1_`** — for models trained on **Training Set 1** * **`T2_`** — for models trained on **Training Set 2** The submission name **must begin exactly with the corresponding prefix**. ### Examples * `T1_baseline_model` * `T2_baseline_model` * `T1_teamname_v03` * `T2_teamname_v03` Participants are strongly encouraged to use a **consistent identifier** (e.g., model name or version number) across the paired `T1_` and `T2_` submissions to facilitate comparison. ### Important Notes * Submissions **not following this naming convention** may be excluded from prize eligibility. * The leaderboard displays all submissions in a single list; however, submissions can be easily filtered using the `T1_` and `T2_` prefixes via the leaderboard search box. * **Winner determination is based solely on the private leaderboard ranking of `T2_` submissions**, in accordance with the competition rules. However, the `T1_` submissions will also be highlighted and published. * **Submissions with missing test images, incorrect labels, or formatting errors** may result in a submission failure.

###🏆 About Challenge###

Pig posture recognition is a key task in Precision Livestock Farming, enabling automated monitoring of animal health and welfare. In this competition, participants develop computer vision models to classify pig postures from 2D images captured under realistic farm conditions, including occlusion, lighting variation, multiple camera views, and pig batches. Using the provided bounding boxes from multi-camera views, participants must predict the posture of each pig instance and submit their results in a standardized submission CSV file. 
Submissions are automatically evaluated, ranked against private leaderboard ground-truth labels, and published on the leaderboard.

The following cash prizes will be awarded based on the final private leaderboard ranking. Please refer to the Rules section for detailed winner selection criteria and prize distribution policies.

  2. Second Prize: $200.00
  3. Third Prize: $100.00

📌 Pig Posture Recognition Competition — FAQ

1. How do I load the dataset and parse the bounding boxes?

You can refer to the multiview_dataset.py provided in the Code section. It shows how to load images, parse bounding boxes, and extract crops.

2. Are test images available?

Yes. Test images are located at:

/kaggle/input/multi-view-pig-posture-recognition/multiview_pig_posture_recognition/test_images/

3. What format should the submission file follow?

Your submission must be a CSV with the following columns:

''' row_id,class_id row_id must match exactly with the IDs in test.csv class_id must be an integer from 0 to 4 Refer to the Data tab for details and an example sample_submission.csv. '''

4. What evaluation metric is used?

The competition uses the F1 Score, which is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall.

5. What is the public/private leaderboard split?

Leaderboard split:

30% Public 70% Private The public score is visible during the competition. Final rankings are determined by the private score.

6. What happens if two participants tie?

This competition follows the standard Kaggle tie-breaking and prize-sharing policy, as described in the Rules section.

To be eligible for a prize:

  • Only the provided pig_posture_recognition dataset may be used
  • No external images or synthetic data are allowed
  • Manual relabeling or extra annotations are not allowed
  • Participants may use external data for non-prize submissions, but such entries are not eligible for awards.

8. Is this a classification or detection task?

This is a bounding-box guided classification task. Bounding boxes are already provided in both train.csv and test.csv. Your model only needs to classify the posture inside the given box. No object detection model is required.

9. Is a baseline notebook provided?

Yes. A full baseline is available in the Code section.

It demonstrates:

  • Parsing bounding boxes
  • Generating posture crops
  • Training a YOLO11 classification model
  • Producing a valid submission.csv

[Private LB 3rd 0.886] DINOv2 Giant (ViT-G/14), LLRD, K-Fold ensemble, TTA

Multi-view Pig Posture Recognition: 3rd Place Solution

Overview

The core of this solution is a DINOv2 Giant (ViT-G/14) trained from its default pretrained weights for 5-class pig posture classification. Predictions are made at the individual pig instance level: each bounding box is cropped from the full image, padded, and resized to 224×224.

Private score: 0.886 (T2), 3rd place. Public score: 0.878 (T2), 4th place.

Model

vit_giant_patch14_reg4_dinov2.lvd142m via timm. I tried several architectures early on (SwinV2, ConvNeXt, DINOv2 variants) and DINOv2 outperformed everything else by a clear margin. Scaling up from DINOv2-S to B to L to G gave consistent gains each step, so I committed to the giant variant for all serious experiments.

Training

K-Fold CV (3-fold). The split is done at the image level, not the row level, so pigs from the same frame always end up in the same fold. Stratification is based on camera type (orb/tur) + dominant class per image. Test predictions are the weighted average of all three fold models, weighted by each fold's best validation F1. OOF macro F1 came out to 0.9508.

Fold best val F1s: 0.9479 / 0.9486 / 0.9406

Layer-wise LR Decay (LLRD). The classification head gets the full learning rate (5e-5) and each transformer block gets 0.85× the rate of the block above it. This made a meaningful difference compared to a flat learning rate.

Loss. A custom PairwisePenaltyLoss wrapping Focal Loss (γ=2.5). Confusion matrix analysis showed that the hardest confusions were Sternal vs. Lateral (54+47 errors) and Sternal vs. Sitting. Penalty weights were set manually based on error counts to push the model harder on those pairs.

Augmentation. Class-specific augmentation policies rather than one-size-fits-all. Sternal_lying gets aggressive rotation (up to 180°) since orientation doesn't matter for that posture. Lateral_left/right get restricted rotation to preserve the directional cue. Sitting gets heavy perspective distortion because it's a small projection under overhead cameras. MixUp (α=0.2) is applied on top.

Other standard ingredients: WeightedRandomSampler (boosting Sternal and Lateral), Model EMA (decay=0.9999), AMP, cosine LR schedule with 3-epoch warmup, early stopping (patience=8).

TTA (8×). 4 rotations × 2 flips. Left/Right labels are swapped appropriately for horizontally flipped passes.

What Didn't Work

Non-DINOv2 architectures: SwinV2 and ConvNeXt fell significantly short of DINOv2, even when comparing similarly sized variants. The gap was large enough that I stopped pursuing them early.

Pseudo-labeling: I tried a two-stage approach where confident test predictions were added back as training data. It hurt performance and was removed entirely.

Every other addition was evaluated incrementally, and each contributed a measurable improvement to the validation F1: LLRD, class-specific augmentation, the custom penalty loss, and TTA were all additive.

What I'd Do Differently

I intentionally left K-Fold to the end, the plan was to finalize the model first and then run K-Fold on the best version since DINOv2-G training is slow. I got too focused on improving the model and by the time I remembered, there was little time left. The peak single-model score was 0.867 at epoch 28, and even with only 3 folds at 22 epochs due to the time constraint, K-Fold pushed the score up to 0.878 which is a really good improvement for this competition. With 4-5 folds at the full 28 epochs the result would likely be higher.

Environment & Hardware

Google Colab PRO, A100 40GB. Train code runs with 38GB VRAM, Inference requires lower VRAM. 3 folds with 22 epochs each and inference took about 12-14 hours.

Public 14th Solution - T2 v46/v49 Candidates, LB 0.854

Public 14th Solution - T2 v46/v49 Candidates, Public LB 0.854

Hi everyone,

I am sharing my public 14th place T2 solution notes for the Multi-view Pig Posture Recognition competition. My best public leaderboard score was 0.854, using the submitted file T2_v46_final_02.csv. I also selected T2_v49_specv1_hgb_cap100.csv as a second final candidate because it was more orthogonal to the main candidate and was designed as a private-leaderboard hedge.

Public code notebook: https://www.kaggle.com/code/junicus/t2-2final-candidates-v46-v49-lb0-854/notebook

Final selected submissions:

  • T2_v46_final_02.csv - public LB 0.854
  • T2_v49_specv1_hgb_cap100.csv - public LB 0.853

1. Overview

This competition was challenging mainly because of the domain shift between training and test data: different time periods, camera views, camera types, lighting conditions, and pig batches. In my experiments, the most difficult errors were around the lying classes, especially the boundary between:

  • Lateral_lying_left
  • Lateral_lying_right
  • Sternal_lying

A large part of the work was not only training stronger classifiers, but also deciding which row-level corrections were reliable enough for the private leaderboard.

2. Base Pipeline

The solution was built around a strong SSL-based visual classifier and several later-stage candidate-generation scripts.

Main ingredients:

  • Bounding-box guided classification only; no detector was trained.
  • Crops were generated from the provided bounding boxes.
  • The main anchor was a DINO/SSL-style image classifier trained on T2.
  • Inference used test-time augmentation with correct left/right label handling for mirrored views.
  • Multiple candidate submissions were generated by blending or selectively grafting row-level decisions.

The final public notebook does not rerun the full training pipeline because the heavy model checkpoints are large. Instead, it packages:

  • final submitted CSV artifacts
  • generation scripts
  • validation/proxy reports
  • checkpoint manifest

This mirrors the common Kaggle deliverable pattern where the notebook documents and reproduces final CSV artifacts from attached packages.

3. What Worked

3.1 Strong Anchor + Conservative Row-Level Grafting

Pure model ensembling saturated around the same public range for me. The biggest useful gains came from conservative row-level changes rather than aggressive retraining.

The best public candidate was:

  • T2_v46_final_02.csv
  • public LB: 0.854

This candidate used a stable anchor and grafted only a limited number of rows from another high-proxy candidate where the local validation/proxy evidence supported the change.

3.2 Shape / Lateral-Sternal Correction

The most useful post-processing family focused on the lateral-vs-sternal boundary. The goal was not to force the class distribution, but to correct low-confidence cases where bbox geometry and model disagreement suggested likely confusion.

Earlier variants in this direction produced the first small public improvement above the plateau.

3.3 Orthogonal Hedge Candidate

The second selected final submission was:

  • T2_v49_specv1_hgb_cap100.csv
  • public LB: 0.853

This candidate used a Sternal/Lateral specialist-style correction. Even though its public score was slightly lower than the main candidate, it disagreed with the main candidate on more rows than other near-identical shape variants. I selected it as a private-LB hedge because public differences of 0.001 were within noise, while diversity between final submissions mattered more.

4. What Did Not Work Well

Several directions did not give reliable improvement for my setup:

  • aggressive pseudo-labeling
  • broader context fine-tuning
  • additional same-family ensembling after the anchor saturated
  • large corrections to Sitting or Standing
  • aggressive class distribution forcing

Most of these produced candidates around 0.851-0.853 public LB, so I treated that as a real plateau and stopped spending submissions on small unvalidated variants.

5. Validation / Selection Strategy

Because public LB represented only part of the test set, I did not choose final submissions purely by public score.

Final selection considered:

  • public LB score
  • candidate disagreement / orthogonality
  • proxy validation reports
  • class distribution sanity checks
  • avoiding aggressive changes to rare or unstable classes

The final pair was chosen as:

  1. Main safe candidate:** T2_v46_final_02.csv
  2. Private hedge candidate:** T2_v49_specv1_hgb_cap100.csv

The idea was that the first candidate should preserve the strongest public score, while the second candidate should cover a different error pattern in case of private leaderboard shake-up.

6. Code Package

The public notebook is here:

https://www.kaggle.com/code/junicus/t2-2final-candidates-v46-v49-lb0-854

It reproduces the two submitted final CSV artifacts from the attached package and writes:

  • /kaggle/working/T2_v46_final_02.csv
  • /kaggle/working/T2_v49_specv1_hgb_cap100.csv
  • /kaggle/working/submission.csv as the primary v46 candidate

The package includes:

  • final submissions
  • candidate generation scripts
  • validation/proxy reports
  • checkpoint manifest

The original competition data is not redistributed; it is used only from the official Kaggle competition dataset.

7. Final Notes

This was a useful competition for learning how fragile public-LB probing can be when the remaining improvements are only a small number of rows. My final approach became more conservative near the end: trust robust candidates, avoid overfitting public noise, and keep the final submissions diverse enough to have a chance on private LB.

Thanks to the organizers for hosting the competition.
